## Two Skies

Every schoolchild learns why sunsets are red: light arriving at a low slant crosses a thick slice of atmosphere, and the atmosphere scatters away its blues, letting the long wavelengths through. What almost nobody mentions is that sunrise and sunset—identical geometry, the same angle, photons traveling essentially the same path—rarely resemble each other at all. Same sun. Different air.

Evening light passes through an atmosphere holding a full day's work. From midmorning onward, heat lifts dust off fields and streets; traffic, chimneys, and pollen add their fine loads; convection stirs everything upward until the lower sky becomes a slow soup of particles. By late afternoon, cumulus has built on the warmth—those photogenic thunderheads are mostly an afternoon accomplishment. When the sun finally drops, its light wades through all of it. The particles strip away more blue, then green, and the result is the saturated amber-and-rose palette we photograph and miss our buses for.

Morning is the sky after housekeeping. Overnight the air stills and cools; dew forms and, forming, pulls a share of the dust down with it; engines rest; gravity does its patient arithmetic. Predawn, when relative humidity peaks and the ground has spent hours radiating heat into space, the atmosphere often reaches its calmest, clearest state—which is part of why serious stargazers guard the last dark hour before sunrise so fiercely. That's when stars stop swimming. And the blue that follows is a cleaner blue than any dusk provides. (Deep basin cities cheat here—nocturnal inversions can bottle the smog till noon—but out in open country, the pattern holds.)

The sailors' rhyme—*red sky at morning, sailors take warning*—turns out not to be folklore but meteorology compressed into meter. In the middle latitudes, weather rolls west to east. A red dawn means the east is clear and morning light is spilling beneath something approaching from the west. A red sunset means the reverse: you're watching light stream through clearing air while it ignites the backs of departing clouds. Without instruments, sailors read direction, speed, and intent out of color alone. It may be the oldest data visualization we possess.

And there's a quieter observation sitting under all the optics. The day accumulates. Everything we burn, kick up, and exhale gathers in the thin layer we live inside, and the evening wears it visibly—the transcript of a day of motion, written in amber. Then night sorts the ledger, and dawn presents us, without comment, an account wiped nearly clean. Not forgiven, exactly—nothing was pardoned, everything is still somewhere—but reset. Each morning begins with a little less of yesterday suspended overhead.

You can test this yourself with nothing more than standing in the same spot twice a day. Take a photograph at the same exposure, twelve hours apart. You will never confuse them. One looks like a beginning.

The other looks like the evidence.
